mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state at least two descriptive words for a given object.
task: Introduce the concept of qualitative properties by showing a wooden block, a plastic cup, and a metal spoon. Guide students to describe how each looks, feels, and smells. Write their descriptive words on the board and explain that these are called properties.

mastery_criterion: Students record at least three accurate qualitative properties for each of the five objects.
task: Set up five observation stations with different everyday materials. Students rotate through the stations, observing the objects and recording three qualitative properties (color, texture, smell) for each in their notebooks.

mastery_criterion: The student lists three appropriate qualitative descriptors, such as brown, hard, and woody smell.
task: Provide each student with a wooden block. Ask them to independently write down three words that describe how it looks, feels, and smells on their assessment sheet.

mastery_criterion: Students can correctly align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object during guided practice.
task: Demonstrate how to use a ruler to measure length in centimeters. Show how to align the zero mark with the edge of the object. Measure a pencil and a book as a class, writing the results with the cm unit.

mastery_criterion: Students accurately measure and record the lengths of at least 8 images within 0.5 cm accuracy.
task: Students work in pairs to measure the length of various printed images of local crops (maize leaves, sugarcane sticks) using a ruler. They record the measurements in centimeters in a structured table.

mastery_criterion: The student writes the correct measurement within 0.5 cm of the actual length and includes cm for all five lines.
task: Give students a worksheet with five printed lines of varying lengths and a ruler. Ask them to measure each line and write the length in centimeters next to it.

mastery_criterion: Students independently align the ruler and read the correct centimeter value.
task: Students retrieve their rulers and measure the length of their own pencils and erasers, recording the values on a sticky note to place on a class chart.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly measure and sequence the strings based on their centimeter length.
task: Provide students with pieces of string of different lengths. They must measure the string in centimeters and order them from shortest to longest on their desks.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the balance scale holds the object with more mass.
task: Introduce the balance scale. Demonstrate how placing objects in the cups causes the scale to tip. Show that the side that goes down has more mass. Compare an apple and a grape as a class.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and record the heavier object for at least 5 pairs using the balance scale.
task: Students work in small groups with a balance scale. They are given pairs of classroom items (e.g., marker vs crayon, scissors vs glue stick). They predict which has more mass, test it, and record the results.

mastery_criterion: The student correctly identifies the object in the cup that goes down as having more mass.
task: Conduct a whole-class demonstration using a balance scale. Place an eraser and a sharpener in the cups. Ask students to independently record on their worksheet which object has more mass based on which cup goes down.

mastery_criterion: Students can explain that quantitative properties use numbers and qualitative properties use descriptive words.
task: Explain the difference between qualitative (words/senses) and quantitative (numbers/measurements) properties. Create a T-chart on the board and sort examples like red, 10 cm, heavy, and 5 grams as a class.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 15 out of 20 property cards and can justify one of each type.
task: Students receive a deck of cards with various properties written and illustrated on them. In pairs, they must sort the cards into Qualitative and Quantitative piles, justifying their choices to each other.

mastery_criterion: All four properties are sorted into the correct categories.
task: Provide a worksheet with a list of properties: red, 15 cm, heavy, 30 degrees. Ask the student to write them into Qualitative and Quantitative columns.

mastery_criterion: Students can match the term malleability to flat objects and ductility to wires.
task: Introduce malleability by flattening a piece of clay or foil, and ductility by showing a copper wire. Explain the definitions and have students repeat the terms while doing hand motions (pressing flat, pulling long).

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify which materials demonstrate malleability and which demonstrate ductility.
task: Students explore stations with safe materials (foil, clay, pipe cleaners). They test if they can flatten them (malleability) or stretch them into wire shapes (ductility) and record their findings on a chart.

mastery_criterion: Both terms are correctly matched to the corresponding material form.
task: Show a picture of aluminum foil and a copper wire on a worksheet. Ask the student to draw a line connecting the correct term (malleability or ductility) to the corresponding picture.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that a color change like rust indicates a chemical property.
task: Show a shiny iron nail and a rusty iron nail. Explain that the color change is evidence of a chemical property reacting to the environment (air/water). Discuss how this is different from just painting the nail.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the apple and the bubbles as chemical changes and justify it using evidence of color change or gas production.
task: Students observe a teacher demonstration of baking soda and vinegar creating bubbles. They then look at pictures of cut apples turning brown and melting ice. They discuss in groups and write down which show chemical properties (bubbles, color change) and justify why.

mastery_criterion: The student selects chemical property and cites the color change or environmental exposure as evidence.
task: Show two images on a worksheet: a shiny metal gate and a rusty metal gate. Ask the student to circle if the material changed due to a physical or chemical property, and write one sentence justifying their choice based on the color change.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain one reason why a cat is living and a rock is not.
task: Introduce the concepts of living and non-living things. Discuss observable traits like needing food, growing, and moving on their own. Create a class chart sorting pictures of a cat, a rock, a tree, and a car.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 10 out of 12 hidden items into the correct categories.
task: Simulate a nature walk using large posters of national protected areas around the room. Students walk around with a clipboard, finding hidden picture cards of entities (animals, plants, rocks, water) and sorting them into a living/non-living T-chart.

mastery_criterion: All four items are placed in the correct categories.
task: Provide a worksheet with a list of words and pictures: dog, rock, tree, bicycle. Ask the student to draw a line to sort them into Living and Non-living boxes.

mastery_criterion: Students independently select and correctly categorize four images.
task: Give students old magazines. They must cut out two pictures of living things and two pictures of non-living things, and glue them onto a divided paper.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the category for 8 out of 10 called items.
task: Conduct a whiteboard relay. Call out an item (e.g., cloud, bird, volcano, grass). Students write L for living or N for non-living on their personal whiteboards and hold them up.

mastery_criterion: Students can repeat the four essential qualities (grow, reproduce, move, feed) when prompted.
task: Explicitly teach the essential qualities of living things: they grow, reproduce, move, and feed. Use a simple story of a puppy growing into a dog, eating food, moving around, and having puppies to illustrate these points.

mastery_criterion: Groups correctly match all scenario cards to the corresponding biological quality.
task: Students work in groups with a set of scenario cards (e.g., a caterpillar eating a leaf, a plant getting taller, a cat with kittens, a dog running). They must match each scenario to the correct quality (feed, grow, reproduce, move).

mastery_criterion: The student circles exactly grow, reproduce, move, and feed.
task: Provide a worksheet with a list of actions: grow, read, reproduce, feed, move, fly. Ask the student to circle the four actions that all living things do.

mastery_criterion: Students can describe the first thing that comes out of a seed (the root).
task: Explain the process of seed germination. Show a time-lapse video (if possible) or a series of large posters showing a seed sprouting roots, then a stem, then leaves. Set up a class demonstration of a bean in a clear cup with wet paper towels.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the 4 stages of germination.
task: Students are given a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the stages of maize germination. They must sequence them in the correct order from dry seed to small plant, and glue them into their notebooks.

mastery_criterion: Drawings show progression: a plain seed, a seed with a small root, and a seed with a larger sprout/leaves.
task: Provide a worksheet with three blank boxes labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5. Ask the student to draw the changes in a germinating bean seed based on what they learned.

mastery_criterion: Students can identify that their fast heartbeat is a response to exercise and pupil change is a response to light.
task: Introduce stimuli and responses. Have students jump in place for 2 minutes and notice their fast heartbeat (internal stimulus/response). Then, use a flashlight to show how a volunteer's pupil shrinks in light (external stimulus/response).

mastery_criterion: Students correctly record at least two stimuli (temperature, light) and their corresponding bodily responses.
task: Students work in pairs to test mild stimuli. One student holds a cup of warm water, then cold water, and describes how their skin feels. Then they observe each other's eyes when covering and uncovering them to see pupil changes. They record the stimuli and responses.

mastery_criterion: The student identifies valid bodily changes (sweat/heartbeat for running, pupil change for light) and links them to the stimuli.
task: Ask the student to write two sentences on a worksheet: what happens to their body when they run fast, and what happens to their eyes in bright light, explaining why these show responses to stimuli.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which objects require batteries or a plug to function.
task: Introduce electrical and non-electrical devices by showing a battery-operated toy car and a wooden push car. Discuss what makes each move. Show pictures of household items and sort them on the board into 'needs electricity' and 'does not need electricity'.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 18 of the 20 objects and accurately record their findings.
task: Students work in small groups to explore a 'mystery box' containing 20 different safe, unplugged everyday objects (e.g., hairbrush, remote control, book, flashlight, spoon, calculator). They must test or examine each object, discuss with their group, and sort them into two physical hoops labeled 'Electrical' and 'Non-Electrical'. They then draw their sorted groups in their science journals.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies at least 4 out of 5 electrical devices from a mixed set of images.
task: Students complete a worksheet with 10 images of household items (television, broom, mobile phone, book, fan, etc.). They must circle the ones that need electrical energy to work.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that the ball dropped from higher up made a bigger hole because it had more energy.
task: Discuss amusement park rides like a slide (tobogán). Ask why sliding from a higher point makes you go faster. Demonstrate dropping a heavy plastic ball into a deep tray of flour from 10 cm and then from 50 cm. Discuss how the higher drop gave the ball more energy, creating a larger crater, just like starting higher on a slide gives more energy.

mastery_criterion: Students accurately record that higher drops cause higher splashes and write a logical conclusion.
task: Students work in pairs with a basin of water and a plastic block. They drop the block from 20 cm, 40 cm, and 60 cm, observing the splash. They use a large piece of chart paper behind the basin to mark how high the water splashed each time. They write a sentence concluding how height affects the splash.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully measure the craters and create a bar graph showing a positive correlation between height and crater size.
task: Students model volcanic rocks falling from different heights. Using a sand tray, they drop pumice stones from various measured heights and measure the width of the impact craters. They create a simple bar graph showing crater width versus drop height.

mastery_criterion: Students draw a larger crater for the 50 cm drop and mention height or energy in their explanation.
task: Flashback activity: Show students a picture of the flour tray experiment from the teach activity. Ask them to draw what the tray looked like after a 10 cm drop versus a 50 cm drop, and write one sentence explaining why they look different.

mastery_criterion: Students select the tall tree coconut and justify it by referencing height and energy.
task: Read a short scenario: 'A coconut falls from a very tall tree, and another falls from a short tree. Which one will hit the sand with more energy?' Students must write their answer and justify it using evidence from past experiments.

mastery_criterion: Student accurately predicts that a higher drop results in more displaced water and justifies it using the concept of mechanical energy.
task: Look at a diagram of two identical spheres, one held 20 cm above a cup of water and one held 60 cm above. Predict which sphere will cause more water to spill and explain why using evidence from class experiments.

mastery_criterion: Students can define conductor as allowing electricity to pass and insulator as blocking it.
task: Build a simple circuit using a 1.5V AA battery, two wires, and a small LED bulb. Leave a gap in the wires. Test a metal paperclip to close the gap (light turns on) and a plastic spoon (light stays off). Introduce the terms conductor and insulator.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly test and classify at least 8 out of 10 objects.
task: Station rotation: Students use safe 1.5V battery circuits to test 10 different classroom objects (eraser, foil, copper wire, wooden block, etc.). They record their predictions and actual results in a T-chart labeled 'Conductors' and 'Insulators'.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully test materials and correctly categorize them as conductors or insulators based on the LED lighting up.
task: Students test various materials (rubber bands, cloth, foil, paper, paperclips) by placing them in a gap in a simple 1.5V battery circuit to see if the LED lights up. They categorize the materials as conductors or insulators based on whether they block or allow electricity to flow.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 given materials into conductors and insulators.
task: Sort a list of materials (copper wire, plastic spoon, human body, rubber eraser, iron nail) into two columns: 'Conducts Electricity' and 'Blocks Electricity'.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally describe that the battery makes the fan blades move.
task: Show a battery-operated fan turning on (electrical to mechanical) and a wind-up toy moving (potential to kinetic). Discuss how energy doesn't disappear but changes its job. Create a simple anchor chart with arrows showing the changes.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all pairs and articulate the transformation happening.
task: Students play a matching card game in pairs. They must match a 'Before' card (e.g., a battery, a wound-up spring) with an 'After' card (e.g., a moving toy car, a spinning fan) and state the energy transformation out loud to their partner.

mastery_criterion: Students identify at least 3 objects and correctly state their energy transformations.
task: Classroom scavenger hunt. Students walk around the room with a clipboard to find 5 objects that transform energy (e.g., pencil sharpener, clock, light switch). They draw the object and write what energy it uses and what it turns into.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 scenarios to their energy transformation.
task: Draw lines to connect the object (e.g., a fan plugged into a wall, a child sliding down a slide) to the correct energy change (e.g., electrical to mechanical, potential to kinetic).

mastery_criterion: Students can explain that the sun's heat caused the ice to melt into liquid water.
task: Place an ice cube in a sealed plastic bag in a sunny window and another in a dark, cool closet. Ask students to predict what will happen. Check back later to see the melted ice. Discuss how adding heat changes solid to liquid, and conceptually discuss boiling water to make gas.

mastery_criterion: Students accurately depict the three states and correctly identify that adding heat causes the changes.
task: Students create a 3-panel comic strip showing the journey of an ice cube. Panel 1: Solid ice. Panel 2: Heat is added (sun or stove), turning it to liquid. Panel 3: More heat is added, turning it to gas. They must write a sentence under each panel explaining the role of heat.

mastery_criterion: Students reason that the heat from the lamp caused the liquid water to turn into a gas.
task: Using the water and sanitation context, students model how heat evaporates water. They place a small amount of water in a shallow dish under a warm desk lamp (representing the sun) and another dish in the shade. They observe and measure the water levels over the session, reasoning why the heated water 'disappears' into gas.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly predicts the state change and justifies it by referencing the addition or removal of heat.
task: Read a short scenario: 'Maria leaves a bowl of ice cubes in the hot sun. What will happen to the ice, and what must she do if she wants to turn that water into a gas?' Write your prediction.

mastery_criterion: Students can identify which object makes a dark shadow and which lets light through.
task: Use a strong flashlight in a darkened room. Shine it through a clear glass cup, a piece of wax paper, and a thick book. Ask students to observe what happens to the light and the shadow on the wall behind each object. Introduce transparent, translucent, and opaque.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully combine opaque and translucent materials to create a functional shadow puppet.
task: Students create a shadow puppet theater. They are given black cardboard (opaque) and colored tissue paper (translucent). They must design a puppet that has both a solid shadow body and glowing colored eyes/features. They test their puppets behind a sheet with a flashlight.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all 5 items based on memory of material properties.
task: Flashback activity: Provide a quick sorting tray with 5 small items (coin, clear plastic cup, wooden block, tissue paper, glass marble). Students must quickly sort them into 'Shadow Makers' and 'Light Passers' based on previous lessons.

mastery_criterion: Students select clear plastic and justify it by stating it lets light pass through.
task: Read a scenario: 'We need to build a greenhouse to help plants grow. Should we use wood or clear plastic for the roof? Why?' Students write their answer recalling that plants need light to pass through.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 materials as light-blocking (opaque) or light-passing (transparent/translucent).
task: Given a list of items (a thick book, a clear glass window, a wooden door, a piece of clear cellophane, a metal spoon), sort them into a table with two columns: 'Forms a dark shadow' and 'Lets light pass through'.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that white light is made of many colors.
task: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass prism onto a white wall to create a rainbow. Discuss how the white light from the flashlight is actually made of many colors, and the prism breaks them apart.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully project a spectrum and record the multiple colors that came from the white light.
task: Students use old CDs and flashlights to explore light decomposition. They shine the light at the back of the CD at different angles to project rainbows onto paper. They trace the colors they see with crayons to document that white light breaks into multiple colors.

mastery_criterion: Students observe and state that spinning the colors makes them look white, showing white light is made of colors.
task: Students create a 'rainbow spinner' (Newton's disc). They color a paper circle with the colors of the rainbow, attach it to a string, and spin it fast. They observe how the colors blend back together to look almost white, reinforcing that white light is a mix of colors.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies that white light can be broken down into multiple colors using a prism.
task: Look at a diagram showing a flashlight shining white light into a glass triangle (prism) and a rainbow coming out the other side. Circle the sentence that best describes what is happening: A) The glass paints the light. B) The light is broken into many colors. C) The light is blocked.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that mixing base colors creates new colors.
task: Demonstrate mixing primary paint colors (cyan, magenta, yellow) in clear cups of water. Show how mixing two colors creates a new color (e.g., yellow and cyan make green). Explain that this is how printers make all the colors in a picture.

mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the new colors created by overlapping the subtractive primary colors.
task: Students are given squares of cyan, magenta, and yellow cellophane. They hold them up to the light in pairs to see what new colors they can make by overlapping them. They record their findings by coloring in overlapping circles on a worksheet.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully mix the primary colors to create green, red, and brown for their painting.
task: Using the local crops context, students must paint a picture of a coffee plant (green leaves, red berries, brown stem) using ONLY cyan, magenta, and yellow paint. They must figure out how to mix the colors on their palette to get the colors they need for the plant.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly describes that mixing a few base colors allows printers to create many different colors.
task: Answer the following question in one sentence: How do inkjet printers make pictures with many different colors if they only use a few ink colors?

mastery_criterion: Students can identify red as danger/stop and green as safe/go.
task: Show large images of local traffic signs (red stop sign) and school emergency exit signs (green). Discuss what the colors mean (red = stop/danger, green = safe/go). Ask students why it is important that everyone agrees on what these colors mean.

mastery_criterion: Students use the correct color for their sign's purpose and state its meaning during their presentation.
task: Students design a safety sign for a local public space (like a park or crosswalk). They must recall and use the correct color: red for a warning/danger sign or green for a safe area/route. They draw the sign and present it, stating the meaning of the color they used.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly apply green for safe routes and red for hazards on their map.
task: Using the seismic risk context, students take a walk around the school to identify evacuation routes and safe zones. They return to the classroom and create a map of the room, using green markers to draw the safe evacuation path and red markers to mark dangerous areas (like heavy bookshelves).

mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches safety colors to their general meanings in a school or community context.
task: Match the color of the sign to its meaning: 1. Red sign with white letters. 2. Green sign with white letters. A) Emergency/Safe route. B) Stop/Danger.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully build a sequence and correctly label at least two energy transformations.
task: Students build a simple sequence using safe classroom objects (e.g., a toy car rolling down a ramp to hit a bell). They draw their sequence and label the energy transformations happening at each step (e.g., potential to kinetic, kinetic to sound).

mastery_criterion: Students can point to the skewer and identify it as the model's axis, and describe that Earth spins on a similar imaginary line.
task: Introduce the concept of Earth's axis by showing a foam ball and inserting a wooden skewer through its center. Explain that the skewer represents an imaginary line called the axis. Spin the ball to demonstrate rotation.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the model and spin it in place rather than moving it in a circle.
task: Students work in pairs to construct their own Earth models using a foam ball and a skewer. They must demonstrate the spinning motion to their partner and explain what the skewer represents.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify opposite ends of the spheres as the poles where the imaginary axis would pass through.
task: Students are given various spherical objects (a plastic ball, a crumpled paper ball, a clay sphere) and must identify where the imaginary axis would be by drawing a line or placing a sticker on the 'poles'.

mastery_criterion: Students draw a vertical or slightly tilted line through the center of both the top and the Earth model in their diagrams.
task: Students compare a spinning top to their Earth model. They spin the top on their desks and draw a diagram showing the imaginary axis of the top compared to the Earth model.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly inserts the axis and spins the model in place, stating the skewer is the imaginary axis.
task: Given a foam ball and a wooden skewer, assemble a model of the Earth and demonstrate its rotation, pointing out the imaginary axis to the teacher.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the globe is experiencing day and which is experiencing night during the demonstration.
task: Darken the room and use a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth. Shine the light on one side of the globe, explaining that the lit side is day and the dark side is night. Slowly rotate the globe to show the cycle.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly rotate the ball in place while keeping the light source stationary, identifying day and night areas.
task: In pairs, students use a small ball on a stick and a small flashlight. One student holds the 'Sun' steady while the other rotates the 'Earth', observing how the light hits the surface.

mastery_criterion: The half of the Earth facing the light source is colored brightly, and the opposite half is colored darkly.
task: Students are given a worksheet with a drawing of the Sun and the Earth. They must color the side of the Earth facing the Sun yellow (day) and the side facing away black or dark blue (night).

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the lit area as day and the shadowed area as night while rotating the globe, keeping the flashlight still.
task: Using a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth, show why it is daytime in one country and nighttime in another by rotating the globe.

mastery_criterion: Students immediately and correctly identify the white side as day and the black side as night.
task: Teacher holds up a ball half-painted white and half-painted black. Teacher asks the class to point to the side experiencing 'day' and the side experiencing 'night'.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all activity cards to the corresponding day or night globe image.
task: Students complete a quick matching card game where they match images of daytime activities with a picture of a sunlit globe, and nighttime activities with a shadowed globe.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that the Sun appears in the East in the morning because of the direction Earth spins.
task: Explain that Earth rotates from West to East. Use a globe and a stationary light source to show how a specific point on the globe enters the light from the East first, making the Sun appear to rise in the East.

mastery_criterion: Students draw long shadows on opposite sides of the block for morning and evening.
task: Students use a small block (representing a building) on a piece of paper. Using a flashlight moving in an arc (to simulate the apparent motion caused by rotation), they trace the shadow of the block in the 'morning' and 'evening'.

mastery_criterion: The Sun is drawn on the East side, and the sentence mentions Earth spinning West to East.
task: Students are given a simple map with East and West labeled. They must draw a Sun on the side where it would appear in the morning and write a one-sentence reason based on Earth's rotation.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that their left side (representing East) enters the light before their face.
task: Students stand in a circle around a central lamp (Sun). They slowly rotate their bodies to the left (West to East) and note which shoulder (East) sees the light first.

mastery_criterion: Prediction is East, justified by demonstrating that the eastern side of a location rotates into the light first on the globe.
task: Based on the fact that Earth rotates from West to East, predict where you will see the Sun in the morning and explain why using your globe model.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that different places have different times because the Sun hits them at different moments.
task: Introduce the concept of time zones. Place a sticker on El Salvador and one on Spain on a globe. Shine a light and rotate the globe, showing that Spain enters the light before El Salvador, meaning their day starts earlier.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that the country to the East experiences morning (and breakfast) first.
task: Students work in pairs with a globe. One points to El Salvador, the other to a country far to the East (like Japan). They rotate the globe into a light source and determine who eats breakfast first.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly deduce that zones to the East are later in the day.
task: Students look at a simplified, color-coded time zone map. They answer questions like: 'If it is noon in the red zone, is it morning or afternoon in the blue zone to the East?'

mastery_criterion: Students choose morning, reasoning that Europe is ahead in time and evening there would be too late.
task: Students are given a scenario where they must call a relative in Europe. They must decide if they should call during their own morning or evening to ensure the relative is awake, justifying their choice based on rotation.

mastery_criterion: Student states it is later in Spain because it is to the East and rotated into the sunlight before El Salvador.
task: Look at a simplified time zone map. If it is 12:00 PM (noon) in El Salvador, determine if it is earlier or later in a country located far to the East, like Spain.

mastery_criterion: Students can define revolution as Earth's path around the Sun and state it takes one year or 365 days.
task: Explain Earth's revolution around the Sun. Place a large yellow ball (Sun) in the center of the room. Walk a smaller globe around the Sun in a large circle, explaining this path is the orbit and takes 365 days (1 year).

mastery_criterion: Students successfully demonstrate both rotation and revolution simultaneously without confusing the two.
task: Students create a floor model of the orbit. One student stands in the center as the Sun. Another student holds a globe and walks the orbital path, ensuring they also spin the globe (rotation) while walking (revolution).

mastery_criterion: The model shows the Earth on a drawn circular/elliptical path around the central Sun, correctly labeled.
task: Students use clay to make a small Sun and a small Earth. They place them on a piece of paper and draw the orbital path with a marker, labeling it '365 days'.

mastery_criterion: Drawing shows Earth circling the Sun, with an arrow indicating the path, labeled '365 days' or '1 year'.
task: Draw a diagram showing the Earth and the Sun. Draw an arrow to show the movement of revolution and label how long one complete movement takes.

mastery_criterion: Students draw a circle or ellipse around a central point representing the Sun.
task: Quick whiteboard activity: Teacher says 'Show me the path of revolution'. Students quickly draw the Sun, Earth, and the orbital path on their mini whiteboards and hold them up.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify true statements about revolution and its 365-day duration.
task: True or False game. Teacher reads statements like 'Earth's orbit takes 1 day' or 'Revolution is when Earth goes around the Sun'. Students stand up for True and sit down for False.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that the extra 6 hours each year add up to a full 24-hour day every four years.
task: Explain that Earth's orbit actually takes 365 days and about 6 hours. Use 4 blocks, each representing 6 hours. Show that over 4 years, these blocks add up to 24 hours, creating one extra day (leap year).

mastery_criterion: Students successfully group the four 6-hour cubes to demonstrate the creation of the extra day.
task: Students work in groups with linking cubes. They build four towers of 365 cubes (represented by a large block) and add one small cube (6 hours) to each. They then combine the 4 small cubes to make a 'new day' block.

mastery_criterion: Students identify the year with 29 days and write that it happens because the extra hours from the orbit added up.
task: Students look at calendars for February over a 5-year period. They must identify the leap year and write a sentence explaining why that specific year has 29 days based on Earth's orbit.

mastery_criterion: Students deduce that without the extra 6 hours, we would never need to add an extra day to February.
task: Students are given a hypothetical scenario: 'What if Earth's orbit took exactly 365 days with no extra hours?' They must write or draw what would happen to our calendar (no leap years).

mastery_criterion: Explanation connects the extra 6 hours of the orbit to the accumulation of a new 24-hour day over four years.
task: Explain why we add an extra day to February every four years, using the exact time it takes Earth to orbit the Sun.

mastery_criterion: Students can name the dry and rainy seasons and identify one visual difference (e.g., green vs brown vegetation).
task: Explain that while some places have four seasons, El Salvador mainly experiences two: the dry season (época seca) and the rainy season (época lluviosa). Show pictures of the local landscape during both seasons.

mastery_criterion: All cards are correctly sorted into the two local seasons.
task: Students sort a series of image cards (umbrellas, dry cracked earth, green lush trees, dusty roads) into two columns: Dry Season and Rainy Season.

mastery_criterion: Students link planting activities that need water to the rainy season.
task: Using the local crops context, students analyze when farmers might plant maize versus when they harvest coffee, linking these activities to the need for water (rainy season) or dry conditions.

mastery_criterion: Drawings accurately reflect the environmental conditions and appropriate clothing for both local seasons.
task: Students create a two-panel drawing. On one side, they draw their school during the dry season; on the other, during the rainy season, including appropriate clothing for themselves in the drawing.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly names the dry and rainy seasons and provides a valid characteristic (e.g., lots of rain, dry dusty ground).
task: Name the two main seasons that are most noticeable in El Salvador and write one characteristic of each.

mastery_criterion: Students can explain that too much water makes the soil loose, leading to landslides during the rainy season.
task: Discuss how intense rain during the rainy season can cause natural hazards like floods and landslides. Show a simple physical model: pour water over a mound of loose soil in a tray to demonstrate a landslide.

mastery_criterion: Students select the steep hill and justify it by stating the rain will wash the loose soil down the slope.
task: Students are given pictures of different landscapes (a steep hill with no trees, a flat paved area, a riverbank). They must decide which area is most vulnerable to a landslide during the rainy season and justify why.

mastery_criterion: Students infer it is the rainy season, reasoning that rivers overflow when there is intense rain.
task: Using the water and sanitation context, students read a short scenario about a town's drinking water pipes breaking due to a river overflowing. They must infer which season this occurred in and explain their reasoning.

mastery_criterion: Student selects the rainy season and justifies it by explaining that intense rain softens the earth, causing the hillside to collapse.
task: Read a short description of a landslide blocking a road. Decide during which season (dry or rainy) this is most likely to happen and justify your answer.

mastery_criterion: Students can point to the roots and stem on a diagram and state their functions in water transport.
task: Introduce plant roots and stems using a pre-prepared celery stalk in colored water to demonstrate water transport.

mastery_criterion: Diagrams correctly label roots for absorption and stems for transport.
task: Draw and label diagrams of local crops, specifically identifying roots and stems.

mastery_criterion: Students explain how their model represents water moving from yarn (roots) up the straw (stem).
task: Build a physical model of a plant using straws for stems and yarn for roots to simulate water transport.

mastery_criterion: All root cards are matched to absorption and stem cards to transport.
task: Sort cards showing different plant parts and match them to their functions (absorption vs transport).

mastery_criterion: Students correctly walk the path and verbally state the function of the part they are standing on.
task: Trace the path of water on a large floor mat depicting a plant, walking from the roots up the stem.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the root as the part that absorbs water and the stem as the part that transports it.
task: Label a provided diagram of a plant with the parts responsible for absorbing and transporting water.

mastery_criterion: Students can identify food and oxygen as the outputs of the process shown on the board.
task: Explain photosynthesis outputs using a felt board model showing sunlight entering and food/oxygen being produced.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly state they are making food and releasing oxygen during the role-play.
task: Role-play the process of photosynthesis where students act as plants producing food and releasing oxygen.

mastery_criterion: Comic strip clearly depicts the plant producing food and oxygen.
task: Create a comic strip showing a plant making its own food and releasing oxygen into the air.

mastery_criterion: Puzzle is assembled correctly with food and oxygen placed as outputs.
task: Assemble a puzzle that shows the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis, focusing on the outputs.

mastery_criterion: Student states that plants make their own food and release oxygen.
task: Write a short explanation of what a plant produces when it makes its own food using sunlight.

mastery_criterion: Students can identify the category for each of the three examples provided.
task: Introduce categories of plant utility (food, medicine, raw materials) using real examples like cotton, mint, and corn.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize their selected local plants into the three utility groups.
task: Create a shopping list for a local market, selecting plants and categorizing them into food, medicine, and raw materials.

mastery_criterion: Poster accurately places at least two local crops into their correct utility categories.
task: Create a poster classifying local crops into food, medicine, and raw materials.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all plant cards to their correct utility category.
task: Play a matching game where students pair a plant with the human need it satisfies (e.g., aloe for medicine, wood for building).

mastery_criterion: Items are correctly sorted into food, medicine, or raw materials based on their plant origin.
task: Sort a mixed basket of everyday items (e.g., wooden spoon, herbal tea box, apple) into plant utility categories.

mastery_criterion: Passes if all provided plants are placed in a plausible utility category.
task: Sort a provided list of plants (e.g., corn, mint, cotton) into categories: food, medicine, and raw materials.

mastery_criterion: Students can state that mushrooms absorb food while plants make it.
task: Compare a mushroom and a plant using photos, focusing on how they get food (making it vs absorbing it).

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify fungi by noting they absorb food from decomposing matter.
task: Analyze case studies of different organisms and justify if they are plants or fungi based on their food source.

mastery_criterion: Student states fungi are not plants and cites their heterotrophic nature and absorptive feeding method.
task: Decide whether a mushroom is a plant or not, and justify your answer using evidence about how it gets its food.

mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct body part on a model when a locomotion type is named.
task: Introduce locomotion types (swim, fly, walk) and corresponding body parts (fins, wings, legs) using animal models.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly match the local animal to its movement and body part.
task: Match common local animals from various Salvadoran environments to their primary movement method and identify the body part used.

mastery_criterion: The drawn animal has clear body parts (e.g., wings) that match the student's stated locomotion method.
task: Design an imaginary animal with specific body parts adapted for a chosen method of locomotion.

mastery_criterion: Cards are sorted correctly and the correct body part is circled on each.
task: Sort animal picture cards by locomotion type and circle the body part that allows it using a dry-erase marker.

mastery_criterion: Chart accurately categorizes animals and lists fins, wings, and legs respectively.
task: Create a chart categorizing animals into swimmers, flyers, and walkers, listing the key body part for each group.

mastery_criterion: Passes if unfamiliar animals are matched correctly with the corresponding body part identified.
task: Given pictures of unfamiliar animals (e.g., an axolotl, an ostrich), infer their primary movement method and circle the body part.

mastery_criterion: Students can define the three diet types based on the pictures shown.
task: Introduce herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores using pictures of animals and their typical meals.

mastery_criterion: Animals are correctly placed into herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore categories.
task: Classify a list of animals into diet categories based on short written descriptions of what they eat.

mastery_criterion: Menus accurately reflect plant-based foods for herbivores, meat for carnivores, and both for omnivores.
task: Create a restaurant menu for different animal types, ensuring the food items match their specific diet classification.

mastery_criterion: All cards/cutouts are placed in the correct diet zone based on prior knowledge of their diets.
task: Sort printed animal cards or student-drawn cutouts into three distinct habitat zones labeled Herbivore, Carnivore, and Omnivore.

mastery_criterion: Cards are sorted correctly within the time limit.
task: Quick sorting of animal diet cards into three piles: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly fill in herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore for each item.
task: Fill-in-the-blank worksheet where students write the correct diet classification next to an animal's name and food source.

mastery_criterion: Passes if all three animals are correctly classified according to their described diets.
task: Read the descriptions of what a cow, a lion, and a bear eat. Classify each as a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore.

mastery_criterion: Students can explain that domestic animals rely on humans while wild animals survive in nature.
task: Define domestic vs. wild animals, focusing on human care and natural habitats, using picture examples.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify wild animals in the scenarios and justify why they should not be pets.
task: Analyze scenarios of finding different animals and justify whether they can be taken home as pets.

mastery_criterion: Students articulate that removing animals harms the ecosystem and the animal's well-being.
task: Group discussion on the impact of taking wild animals from national protected areas to keep as pets.

mastery_criterion: Brochure includes at least one valid reason (e.g., need for space, natural diet) why wild animals shouldn't be pets.
task: Create an informational brochure explaining why wild animals are not pets, using evidence about their needs.

mastery_criterion: Needs are correctly sorted, demonstrating understanding of the difference in survival strategies.
task: Sort a list of animal needs into 'Provided by Humans' (domestic) and 'Found in Nature' (wild).

mastery_criterion: Passes if the student decides against keeping the wild animal and provides a justification based on its natural habitat.
task: Decide whether a monkey found in the forest should be taken home as a pet. Justify your answer using evidence.

mastery_criterion: Students can name at least one human threat and one corresponding protective action.
task: Discuss human threats to wildlife (e.g., littering, feeding) and introduce concrete conservation actions.

mastery_criterion: Rules directly address mitigating human threats (e.g., no littering, stay on trails).
task: Draft a set of rules for visitors to national protected areas to ensure wild animals are protected.

mastery_criterion: Students acting as rangers clearly state a rule that protects wildlife during the role-play.
task: Role-play park rangers explaining conservation rules to visitors who are acting carelessly.

mastery_criterion: Sign includes a clear visual and text rule that protects wildlife.
task: Design a warning sign for a forest to remind people how to protect the animals living there.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly match the consequence and propose a protective alternative action.
task: Match scenarios of human actions in nature to their consequences for wildlife, then propose a better action.

mastery_criterion: Passes if the response correctly identifies the harm of feeding wild animals and proposes a safe alternative like observing.
task: Read a scenario where a visitor wants to feed a wild animal. Write a response explaining why they shouldn't and what they should do instead.

mastery_criterion: Students can point to and name the roots, stem, and leaves on the live plant.
task: Introduce the basic parts of a plant (roots, stem, leaves) using a live potted plant.

mastery_criterion: Drawing includes roots, stem, and leaves, all correctly labeled.
task: Draw a plant and label its basic parts (roots, stem, leaves).

mastery_criterion: Students can name one useful and one harmful aspect of fungi.
task: Introduce the uses of fungi (e.g., food, medicine) and their potential harms (e.g., diseases, toxicity) using pictures.

mastery_criterion: Cards are correctly sorted into helpful and harmful categories.
task: Sort scenario cards into 'Helpful Fungi' and 'Harmful Fungi' categories.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully wrap the string, mark it accurately, and read the measurement on the ruler within 1 cm of accuracy.
task: Demonstrate how to wrap a string around a spherical fruit, mark the meeting point, and measure the string segment with a ruler. Have students replicate the process with an orange.

mastery_criterion: Students record at least 5 accurate measurements, demonstrating proper string alignment and ruler usage.
task: Students work in pairs to measure the circumference of various classroom objects (globes, balls, thick markers) using string and rulers, recording their data in a table.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the crop with the largest circumference based on their accurate string measurements.
task: Students measure the circumference of different local crops (like small pumpkins or large maize cobs) using string and rulers to determine which crop has the largest girth.

mastery_criterion: The recorded measurement is within 1 cm of the actual circumference and the string method is used correctly.
task: Provide students with a spherical fruit, a piece of string, and a ruler. Ask them to determine the distance around the thickest part of the fruit and record the measurement in centimeters.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble a hanger balance that hangs level when empty.
task: Guide students step-by-step to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups. Demonstrate how to find equilibrium using identical marbles.

mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the number of marbles required to balance at least 4 different objects.
task: Students use their constructed balances to compare the mass of various classroom items (erasers, pencils, glue sticks) against a standard non-standard unit (marbles), recording the equivalents.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully balance the items with coins and record the mass in 'coin units'.
task: Students use their balances to determine the mass of hypothetical household items purchased with a hypothetical dollar budget, using coins as the non-standard mass unit.

mastery_criterion: The balance is constructed symmetrically and the student correctly identifies the equilibrium point with the correct number of marbles.
task: Ask students to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups, and then determine how many marbles equal the mass of a small eraser.

mastery_criterion: Students assemble the balance correctly and achieve equilibrium within the time limit.
task: Students quickly reassemble a balance from disassembled parts and verify its equilibrium using identical wooden blocks.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly add beads one by one until the hanger is level.
task: Students use a pre-made balance to find the mass of a small rock in terms of plastic beads, recalling the procedure for achieving equilibrium.

mastery_criterion: Students can articulate that the folded bridge holds more weight and identify the folds as the reason for increased strength.
task: Demonstrate how to build a flat paper bridge and a fan-folded paper bridge between two books. Show how to add coins to the center until collapse.

mastery_criterion: Students record data accurately and reason that more folds generally increase structural resistance up to a point.
task: Students experiment with different numbers of folds in their paper bridges (e.g., 2 folds vs. 6 folds) and record how many coins each can hold, justifying which design is best.

mastery_criterion: Students justify the folded design's strength using evidence from their block count data.
task: Students test flat vs. folded bridges using small blocks instead of coins, simulating a road over a water sanitation channel, and write a justification for the strongest design.

mastery_criterion: The student records that the folded bridge holds significantly more coins and justifies that the folds make the paper stiffer.
task: Have students place coins one by one on the center of a flat paper bridge until it collapses, then repeat with a fan-folded bridge, and state which design is stronger and why based on data.

mastery_criterion: Students explicitly link the visual observation of the melting wax to the generation of heat, stating that electrical energy from the battery transforms into thermal energy.
task: Perform a teacher-led demonstration connecting a battery to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Have students observe the wax melting as a visual indicator of heat and identify the energy change.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify electrical to thermal energy for the graphite, and electrical to mechanical/light for the others.
task: Students observe a series of safe, teacher-led demonstrations (e.g., a small battery-operated fan, a flashlight, and the graphite circuit) and identify the energy transformations in each.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the input (electrical) and output (thermal) energy for at least 3 appliances.
task: Students review diagrams of household appliances (toaster, iron, heater) and identify that they all transform electrical energy into thermal energy, similar to the graphite experiment.

mastery_criterion: The student states that electrical energy from the battery is changing into thermal energy (heat) in the pencil lead, using the melting wax as evidence.
task: Show students a safe, teacher-led demonstration of a battery connected to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Ask them to observe the wax melting and name the type of energy transformation occurring.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the device and demonstrate that twisting the rubber band causes it to roll.
task: Guide students to build a rolling device using CDs, a cardboard tube, and rubber bands. Demonstrate how twisting the rubber band stores energy for motion.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully operate the device and record that more twists result in a longer rolling distance.
task: Students experiment with their elastic devices by twisting the rubber band a specific number of times (e.g., 5, 10, 15) and measuring how far the device rolls.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully modify the device, operate it, and observe changes in motion.
task: Students modify their elastic devices by adding weight (e.g., taping coins to the tube) to see how mass affects the motion generated by the twisted rubber band.

mastery_criterion: The device is assembled correctly and demonstrates motion upon release.
task: Instruct students to build a rolling device using CDs, a cardboard tube, and rubber bands, twist the rubber band mechanism, and release it on the floor to demonstrate motion.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state the difference between domestic and wild animals based on human reliance.
task: Present images of common animals. Explain the difference between domestic (rely on humans) and wild (survive independently). Sort a few examples together on the board.

mastery_criterion: Groups correctly sort at least 18 out of 20 cards based on human reliance.
task: Students work in small groups to sort a deck of 20 animal cards into 'domestic' and 'wild' piles, discussing their reasoning for each.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the food source (human provided vs. independently found).
task: Students draw one domestic animal and one wild animal found in El Salvador (e.g., iguanas, tacuacines, or various birds), writing one sentence for each explaining how it gets its food.

mastery_criterion: All animals are correctly categorized and the reasoning references human dependence vs. independent survival.
task: Provide a list of animals (e.g., dog, chicken, iguana, bee). Ask the student to sort them into 'domestic' and 'wild' categories and provide one reason for their sorting.

mastery_criterion: Students consistently move to the correct side of the room based on the animal's classification.
task: Play a quick game where the teacher calls out an animal name and students move to the left side of the room for 'domestic' and the right side for 'wild'.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw lines matching the animals to their appropriate habitat icons.
task: Students complete a quick matching worksheet connecting pictures of animals to either a 'house/farm' icon (domestic) or a 'forest/jungle' icon (wild).

mastery_criterion: Students successfully cut straws to the correct length and pack them so they do not fall out when the can is inverted.
task: Demonstrate how to measure and cut paper straws to the length of a recycled can, and pack them tightly inside to create hollow spaces for insects.

mastery_criterion: Students adapt their packing technique to the new shape, ensuring materials are secure and provide hollow spaces.
task: Students build a second insect hotel using a different container shape (e.g., a square milk carton) and natural materials like hollow twigs, ensuring tight packing.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully attach natural camouflage to the exterior without blocking the hollow tube entrances.
task: Students decorate the outside of their insect hotels using natural materials (leaves, bark) glued to the exterior to help it blend into a natural environment.

mastery_criterion: The tubes are cut to size and packed tightly enough to stay in place when the can is tilted.
task: Ask students to create an insect shelter by cutting paper straws to the length of a recycled can and packing them tightly inside.

mastery_criterion: Students verbally identify the quiet garden and reason that insects avoid human disturbance.
task: Discuss why insects need quiet places. Show pictures of a busy playground and a quiet garden corner, asking students to infer which is better for an insect hotel and why.

mastery_criterion: Students select a viable low-traffic spot and note its quiet nature on their map.
task: Take students on a walk around the schoolyard. Have them select a specific spot for their insect hotel and draw a map marking the location, noting why it is low-traffic.

mastery_criterion: Students place the 'X' away from paths and playgrounds, justifying it with the need to avoid disturbance.
task: Students review a map of a hypothetical park and mark an 'X' where they would place an insect hotel, writing a justification based on avoiding human paths.

mastery_criterion: The chosen location is low-traffic and the justification explicitly mentions avoiding disturbance to the insects.
task: Ask students to choose a location in the schoolyard or at home to place their insect hotel and write one sentence explaining why that location is best for the insects.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully replicate the layers (rocks, then soil) and plant their specimen securely.
task: Demonstrate how to layer small rocks for drainage, add soil, and carefully plant a small specimen in a clear plastic container to create a terrarium.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully water the plant without flooding it, observing the drainage layer's function.
task: Students add decorative elements (small plastic animals, colored stones) to their terrariums and lightly water the soil, observing how the water drains into the rock layer.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly layer rocks and soil, and plant the seed at the correct depth.
task: Students build a second, smaller terrarium using a plastic cup, focusing on planting a seed (like maize) instead of a live plant, ensuring the soil depth is appropriate.

mastery_criterion: The terrarium has distinct layers (rocks then soil) and the plant is securely placed in the soil with roots covered.
task: Provide students with a clear plastic container, small rocks, soil, and a small plant. Ask them to assemble a terrarium that supports the plant's growth.

mastery_criterion: Student points to and names at least three objects that pose a risk in the poster.
task: Display a large poster of a messy classroom. Guide students to point out objects that could cause someone to trip, fall, or get hurt. Discuss why each identified object is a risk.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts all unsafe situation cards into the risk pile.
task: Students sort illustrated cards into two piles: safe situations and unsafe situations (risks).

mastery_criterion: Student circles at least three distinct risks across the provided photographs.
task: Students view photographs of different rooms in a house and circle the accident risks using a dry-erase marker.

mastery_criterion: Student successfully draws three recognizable risks and identifies the risks in their partner's drawing.
task: Students draw a picture of a playground and intentionally include three accident risks, then trade with a partner to find them.

mastery_criterion: Student circles a spilled liquid, an open cabinet door, and a tripping hazard.
task: Provide a worksheet with an image of a messy kitchen. Students must independently circle three things that could cause an accident.

mastery_criterion: Student can verbally state that the tower is the hazard and standing close is the risk.
task: Bridge the concept of physical risks (like tripping, learned previously) to natural events. Use wooden blocks to build a tall, unstable tower representing a local hazard (like the San Salvador volcano or a local fault line). Place a toy figure far away, then close to it. Explain that the hazard is the event itself, but the risk (probability of harm) changes based on where the figure stands.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly pairs the hazard cards with their corresponding risk definition cards.
task: Students match cards showing a natural event (hazard) with cards showing the probability of harm (risk) based on human location.

mastery_criterion: Student holds up the correct card for at least 4 out of 5 scenarios.
task: Read scenarios about local Salvadoran hazards (e.g., earthquakes on the San Salvador fault, heavy rains in vulnerable areas). Students hold up a red card if the scenario describes a hazard, and a yellow card if it describes a risk.

mastery_criterion: Student selects the option defining risk as the probability of suffering harmful consequences.
task: Students complete a multiple-choice question selecting the correct definition of 'risk' from three options.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the difference through physical movement.
task: Quick recall game: The teacher says a word (either a hazard like 'rain' or a risk like 'flooded house'). Students stand up for hazard, sit down for risk.

mastery_criterion: Student's sentence includes the concept of probability of harm or getting hurt.
task: Exit ticket: Students write or dictate one sentence explaining what a risk is before leaving for recess.

mastery_criterion: Student successfully demonstrates dropping, covering their head/neck, and holding onto a sturdy object.
task: Demonstrate the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold on' technique for earthquakes. Explain each step clearly. Have students practice the motion step-by-step under their desks.

mastery_criterion: Student reacts promptly and correctly assumes the safe position without prompting.
task: Role-play activity: The teacher calls out 'Earthquake!' at random times during a 30-minute period. Students must immediately execute the safe action.

mastery_criterion: Student's comic accurately depicts a recognized safety measure in the middle panel.
task: Students create a simple three-panel comic strip showing a character feeling an earthquake, taking cover, and waiting safely.

mastery_criterion: Student places the evacuation steps in a logical, safe order for the given hazard.
task: Students sequence a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the steps of an emergency evacuation plan for various hazards, including earthquakes, floods, and landslides.

mastery_criterion: Student draws or writes about a recognized safety measure for floods, such as moving to higher ground.
task: Present a novel scenario: a heavy rainstorm causes a flood warning near their home. Students draw or write one safe action they should take in this specific context.

mastery_criterion: Student states that the roots hold the soil, preventing it from washing away.
task: Relate the activity to local issues like landslides in Nejapa or sedimentation of the Lempa River. Set up three plastic bottle halves: one with bare soil, one with dead leaves, one with live plants. Pour equal amounts of water through each. Ask students to observe the runoff water color and infer why the plant bottle has clear water, protecting the 'hillside'.

mastery_criterion: Student infers that a steeper angle causes more soil to wash away, but plants still offer the best protection.
task: Students repeat the erosion model experiment, but this time they tilt the bottles at a steeper angle to simulate a steep hill. They observe and discuss how the angle affects the amount of soil washed away.

mastery_criterion: Student reasons that faster water flow carries more soil away.
task: Students test the erosion model by pouring water very slowly (light rain) versus very quickly (heavy storm) into the bare soil bottle, comparing the runoff.

mastery_criterion: Student observes and states which soil type resulted in dirtier runoff water.
task: Students compare the erosion of regular garden soil versus sandy soil in the bare-soil model, observing which washes away faster.

mastery_criterion: Student selects the bare dirt hill and provides a logical justification involving the lack of roots to hold the soil.
task: Show the student a picture of a steep, bare dirt hill and a picture of a hill covered in grass and trees. Ask them to predict which hill will lose more soil during a heavy rainstorm and explain why using their knowledge of roots.

mastery_criterion: Student can correctly identify the bin for an apple core and a plastic bottle during the demonstration.
task: Introduce the concepts of biodegradable (nature breaks it down) and non-biodegradable (nature cannot easily break it down). Show clean examples of each and sort them into two labeled bins as a class.

mastery_criterion: Student places their assigned cards in the correct hoops.
task: Relay race: Students pick a picture card of a waste item from a pile and run to drop it in the correct biodegradable or non-biodegradable hoop.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 5 items on their T-chart.
task: Students cut out pictures of various items from old magazines and paste them onto a T-chart labeled Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable.

mastery_criterion: Student includes only biodegradable items (like fruit peels, leaves, paper) on their mobile.
task: Students create a hanging mobile using only drawings of biodegradable items, reinforcing what belongs in that specific category.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly connects the apple core and banana peel to biodegradable, and the plastic bottle and glass jar to non-biodegradable.
task: Provide a worksheet with images of an apple core, plastic bottle, glass jar, and banana peel. Students draw a line connecting each item to the correct bin (Biodegradable or Non-biodegradable).

mastery_criterion: Student identifies that not washing hands after the bathroom was the poor hygiene practice.
task: Read a short story about a character who forgets to wash their hands after using the bathroom and gets a stomach ache. Discuss the specific action that caused the illness.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly circles the poor hygiene practices (e.g., sneezing into hands, not washing hands).
task: Show a series of pictures depicting daily routines. Students must spot and circle the 'mistake' (the poor hygiene practice) in each picture.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the acted-out habit as poor hygiene when applicable.
task: Play a game of charades where students act out either a good hygiene habit or a poor hygiene habit. The class guesses the action and states if it is good or poor.

mastery_criterion: Student places cards like 'not washing hands' into the 'Can make us sick' pile.
task: Students sort a deck of cards showing various actions into a 'Keeps us healthy' pile and a 'Can make us sick' pile.

mastery_criterion: Student marks a sad face for 'Not washing hands after going to the bathroom'.
task: Read a list of actions aloud. Students mark a sad face on their paper next to the number if the action represents poor hygiene.

mastery_criterion: Student can state that vaccines help make defenses to fight sickness.
task: Explain vaccines using a metaphor: the body is a castle, and vaccines are training for the guards (defenses) so they know how to fight off invaders (sickness).

mastery_criterion: Student's drawing reflects the concept of protection or defense inside the body.
task: Students draw a picture of their body's 'defenses' (like tiny shields or guards) stopping sickness, based on the vaccine metaphor.

mastery_criterion: Student places the pictures in the correct chronological order.
task: Students sequence three pictures: 1) Getting a vaccine, 2) Body making defenses, 3) Staying healthy when sickness is around.

mastery_criterion: Student writes that a vaccine helps the body make defenses or fight off sickness.
task: Ask the student to write one sentence explaining what a vaccine does inside the body.

mastery_criterion: Student recalls a relevant word associated with vaccine function.
task: Pass a soft ball around a circle. When the music stops, the student holding the ball must say one word related to what vaccines do (e.g., 'defenses', 'protect', 'fight').

mastery_criterion: Student fills in the blank with 'defenses' or a similar accurate term.
task: Provide a quick fill-in-the-blank slip: 'A vaccine helps the body make ________ to fight sickness.'

mastery_criterion: Student can point to the foods that require cooking when asked.
task: Show pictures of raw chicken, raw beans, and an apple. Explain that while the apple can be washed and eaten raw, the chicken and beans must be cooked to be safe to eat.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly places items like play-chicken in the 'Must be cooked' basket.
task: Students sort plastic play-food into two baskets: 'Safe to eat raw (after washing)' and 'Must be cooked'.

mastery_criterion: Student draws and correctly identifies which of their drawn items needs cooking.
task: Students draw a 'safe menu' consisting of one item that can be eaten raw and one item that must be cooked, labeling them appropriately.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches the raw ingredients to their cooked counterparts.
task: Matching game: Students match a picture of a raw ingredient (like raw meat or raw dough) to its safe, cooked final dish.

mastery_criterion: Student circles the raw chicken and raw beans.
task: Provide a worksheet with images of raw chicken, an apple, and raw beans. Students circle the ones that must be cooked before eating.

mastery_criterion: Student reasons that hands must be washed with soap to remove invisible organisms that spread.
task: Rub a drop of cooking oil and a pinch of ground cinnamon on a student's hand to represent invisible organisms. Have them try to wash it off with just water, then with soap and water. Discuss why soap is needed to break down the oils that trap dirt and germs, justifying the need for proper handwashing.

mastery_criterion: Student infers that soap is needed to properly remove the 'invisible organisms' represented by the cinnamon.
task: Students work in pairs. One applies the oil and cinnamon 'germs'. They test washing with cold water only, warm water only, and finally soap and water, observing which method removes the 'germs' best and inferring why soap is essential.

mastery_criterion: Student's sentence justifies handwashing by mentioning the removal of organisms or germs.
task: Students trace their hand on paper and draw tiny 'invisible organisms' all over it, then write one sentence at the bottom explaining why they need to wash them off.

mastery_criterion: Student's letter includes the reasoning that invisible things can make us sick.
task: Students dictate or write a short letter to a friend explaining why they should use soap when washing hands, even if their hands don't look dirty.

mastery_criterion: Student identifies the dish with growth and explains that invisible organisms from unwashed hands were transferred to it.
task: Show the student pictures of two petri dishes from a handwashing experiment (one with spots of bacterial growth, one clean). Ask them to infer which dish was touched by unwashed hands and justify their answer based on the presence of invisible organisms.

mastery_criterion: Student can explain their role as a defense created by the vaccine.
task: Students role-play as 'body guards' (defenses) learning to recognize a 'villain' (sickness) after being trained by a 'teacher' (vaccine).

mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least four food items.
task: Students create a 'safe kitchen' poster by cutting out pictures of food and gluing them under 'Wash and Eat' or 'Cook First' headings.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly states the unit used for mass, volume, and length when prompted.
task: Introduce standard units (g, L, cm) by displaying common household items and explicitly teaching which unit corresponds to mass, volume, and length.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts at least 8 out of 10 items into the correct measurement station.
task: Students sort a variety of everyday items into stations based on whether they are measured in grams, pounds (libras), liters, or centimeters, discussing local market contexts.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 4 out of 5 items to their appropriate measurement unit.
task: Students complete a matching task where they draw lines connecting 5 drawn items (milk, cereal, pencil, water bottle, rope) to their correct unit (L, g, cm).

mastery_criterion: Student can verbally explain the importance of starting at the zero mark.
task: Demonstrate how to align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object and read the measurement in centimeters.

mastery_criterion: Student records measurements that are within +/- 0.5 cm of the actual length.
task: Students work in pairs to measure and record the length of 5 specific classroom objects (e.g., desk edge, book, pencil) in centimeters.

mastery_criterion: Student measures both objects accurately to the nearest centimeter (+/- 0.5 cm).
task: Students independently measure the length of a provided sticky note and a pencil using a ruler, recording their answers in centimeters.

mastery_criterion: Student can articulate that different scales have different sensitivities.
task: Show a bathroom scale and a kitchen scale. Place a spoonful of salt on both to demonstrate that the bathroom scale does not register the small mass.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts items and provides a valid reason based on the object's mass.
task: Students are given cards with pictures of various items (e.g., a single coffee bean, a sack of basic grains like beans or rice) and must sort them by which scale is appropriate, justifying their choice.

mastery_criterion: Student selects kitchen scale and states the bathroom scale is not sensitive enough for small masses.
task: Students write a short paragraph choosing whether to use a bathroom scale or a kitchen scale to measure a spoonful of salt, explaining their reasoning.

mastery_criterion: Student can explain why the broken ruler gives a false reading.
task: Present a ruler with the first 2 cm snapped off. Demonstrate how measuring a 5 cm object with it gives an incorrect reading if not adjusted, explaining reliability.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies damaged tools as unreliable and links the damage to inaccurate readings.
task: Students inspect a 'toolkit' of various measuring devices (some intact, some intentionally damaged like a stretched measuring tape) and categorize them as reliable or unreliable, writing a reason for each.

mastery_criterion: Student states it is unreliable and links the missing starting point to incorrect measurements.
task: Students look at a picture of a ruler missing the zero mark and write whether it is reliable for measuring, explaining why.

mastery_criterion: Student identifies it as unreliable because the missing part prevents accurate mass measurement.
task: Quick recall: Show an image of a kitchen scale with a missing weighing pan. Ask students to write down if it is reliable and why.

mastery_criterion: Student can define a force as a push or a pull that changes motion.
task: Introduce forces as pushes and pulls using a toy car. Demonstrate pushing to start, pulling to move closer, and pushing/pulling to stop the car.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the force in at least 4 out of 5 acted scenarios.
task: Students act out various scenarios (e.g., opening a door, pressing a button, tug-of-war) and the class identifies the primary force as a push or pull.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly classifies at least 4 out of 5 actions.
task: Students classify a written list of 5 actions (kicking a ball, stopping a rolling ball, pressing a doorbell, pulling a wagon, closing a drawer) as a push or a pull.

mastery_criterion: Student can state that friction opposes motion and makes objects stop faster on rougher surfaces.
task: Slide a book across a smooth table and then across a piece of carpet. Ask students to predict and observe the difference. Explicitly teach that friction is the force opposing the motion, causing it to stop faster on rough surfaces.

mastery_criterion: Student identifies that rougher surfaces apply more friction, stopping the car sooner.
task: Students roll toy cars down a ramp onto different surfaces (tile, towel, sandpaper) and measure how far they go, identifying friction as the stopping force.

mastery_criterion: Student predicts sandpaper and explicitly names friction as the opposing force.
task: Students read a scenario about a toy car rolling on glass versus sandpaper, predict which surface stops it faster, and write an explanation using the concept of friction.

mastery_criterion: Student can explain that objects with more mass require more force to move.
task: Demonstrate pushing an empty cardboard box versus a box filled with heavy books across the floor. Introduce the dynamometer as a tool to measure the force applied. Discuss why the heavier box requires more effort.

mastery_criterion: Student concludes that the rubber band stretches more (more force) for the object with more mass.
task: Students use a rubber band or a simple dynamometer to pull different objects (a wooden block, a block with weights) and observe the force required, relating it to mass.

mastery_criterion: Student selects the heavier box and explicitly links the required force to the object's mass.
task: Students read a scenario about an empty box and a box full of books, predict which requires more force to push, and explain why.
