mastery_criterion: Student successfully observes and understands the steps to coil wire around a nail and connect it to a battery.
task: Demonstrate how to tightly coil insulated copper wire around an iron nail, strip the ends, and connect them to a AA battery to create an electromagnet that picks up paperclips.

mastery_criterion: Student successfully coils wire around a nail, connects it to a battery, and picks up at least two paperclips.
task: Students assemble their own electromagnets following the demonstrated procedure and test how many paperclips they can lift.

mastery_criterion: Student successfully alters the number of coils and records the new lifting capacity.
task: Students rebuild their electromagnets with half the number of wire coils and test if it changes the number of paperclips they can lift.

mastery_criterion: Pass if the device successfully attracts paperclips when connected and drops them when disconnected.
task: Assemble an electromagnet using the provided materials and demonstrate its ability to attract at least two paperclips to the teacher.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies and labels the components needed for a large-scale electromagnet.
task: Students design a hypothetical crane system on paper that uses an electromagnet to move scrap metal, labeling the battery, coil, and core.

mastery_criterion: Student understands that disconnecting the circuit stops the current, which eliminates the magnetic field.
task: Demonstrate an electromagnet holding paperclips, then disconnect one wire to show the paperclips falling. Explain that the magnetic field depends entirely on the flow of electric current.

mastery_criterion: Student predicts and verifies that opening the switch stops the current and drops the paperclips.
task: Students integrate a switch into their electromagnet circuit and predict how the switch will control the magnetic field, then test their prediction.

mastery_criterion: Student reasons that without current, the domains in the soft iron nail randomize again, losing the strong magnetic field.
task: Students disconnect their electromagnets and test if the iron nail retains any slight magnetism by trying to pick up a single iron filing, then justify why it is mostly non-magnetic.

mastery_criterion: Pass if the student states the paperclips fall and links this to the cessation of electric current.
task: What will happen to the paperclips attached to your electromagnet if you disconnect one wire from the battery? Justify your answer.

mastery_criterion: Student justifies the analogy, explaining that stopping the flow stops the action in both systems.
task: Students compare an electromagnet controlled by a switch to a water valve controlled by a handle, justifying how both require an active flow (current or water) to perform work.

mastery_criterion: Student understands that the circuit must be broken to insert the multimeter in series.
task: Demonstrate how to open a simple circuit and connect a multimeter in series to measure the electrical current, ensuring students understand the difference between series and parallel connections for measurement.

mastery_criterion: Student successfully measures and records the current without short-circuiting the battery.
task: Students build a simple circuit with a resistor and battery, then open the circuit to measure the current with a multimeter.

mastery_criterion: Pass if the student opens the circuit, connects the multimeter in series, and gets a valid reading.
task: Given a functioning simple circuit, the student must correctly measure the current flowing through it.

mastery_criterion: Student can identify which parts of the circuit are in series and which are in parallel.
task: Demonstrate how to build a mixed circuit (one resistor in series with two in parallel) on a breadboard and measure its equivalent resistance.

mastery_criterion: Student correctly assembles the circuit and measures the equivalent resistance.
task: Students build a mixed circuit using three resistors and measure the total equivalent resistance with a multimeter.

mastery_criterion: Students can correctly identify the number of valence electrons for at least five different representative elements.
task: Introduce the concept of valence electrons using a large periodic table. Guide students to find the group number and correlate it with the number of valence electrons for representative elements.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all element cards to their correct valence electron counts without teacher assistance.
task: Students work in groups to create a card sorting game where they match element cards with their corresponding valence electron count cards, then play the game to reinforce memory.

mastery_criterion: Worksheet is completed with 90% accuracy and the periodic table is correctly color-coded by group.
task: Students complete a comprehensive worksheet identifying valence electrons for 15-20 different elements, then color-code a blank periodic table based on valence electron counts to identify patterns.

mastery_criterion: Students score at least 8 out of 10 correct identifications.
task: Administer a written quiz where students must state the number of valence electrons for Carbon, Oxygen, Sodium, and seven other representative elements using a standard periodic table.

mastery_criterion: Students consistently hold up the correct number within 5 seconds.
task: Flashcard rapid-fire session where the teacher holds up an element symbol and students write the valence electron number on a mini-whiteboard.

mastery_criterion: 100% correct matching on the paper activity.
task: Students complete a quick matching activity on paper, connecting 15 element symbols to their valence electron numbers from memory.

mastery_criterion: Students can replicate the Lewis structure for H2O and one other simple molecule on their own paper.
task: Demonstrate how to draw Lewis structures for atoms and simple molecules like H2O, emphasizing the octet rule and electron pairing.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly build and draw at least 8 out of 10 assigned molecular structures.
task: Students use small beads or buttons to represent electrons and build Lewis structures for a list of 10 simple molecules on paper mats, then draw the final structures.

mastery_criterion: Accurate drawings showing correct octets and duets for all atoms in the packet.
task: Students complete a comprehensive packet drawing Lewis structures for various molecules, identifying bonding pairs and lone pairs.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw the structures, satisfying the octet/duet rules and correctly labeling pairs.
task: Students are given a list of 5 chemical formulas and must draw the complete Lewis structure for each, explicitly labeling bonding and non-bonding pairs.

mastery_criterion: Students can verbally justify why NaCl is ionic and O2 is covalent based on element types.
task: Briefly review the location of metals and non-metals on the periodic table. Explain the difference between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds based on electron transfer or sharing. Model how to predict bond type using the periodic table.

mastery_criterion: Correct prediction and logical justification for at least 80% of the compounds.
task: Students analyze a list of hypothetical and real compounds, predict their bond types, and write a short justification for each based on electron behavior.

mastery_criterion: Posters accurately categorize all substances and include clear, correct reasoning for each category.
task: Students create a poster categorizing 20 different substances into ionic, covalent, or metallic bonds, including a written explanation of the rules used to categorize them.

mastery_criterion: Correct predictions for all 10 pairs and scientifically accurate justifications for the 3 selected pairs.
task: Written exam where students must predict the bond type for 10 pairs of atoms and provide a written justification for 3 selected pairs explaining the electron transfer or sharing.

mastery_criterion: Students can identify a tetrahedral shape from a physical model and state that it minimizes repulsion.
task: Introduce VSEPR theory using balloons tied together to show how electron pairs repel each other to form 3D shapes like tetrahedral, linear, and bent.

mastery_criterion: Models accurately reflect the 3D geometry and are correctly labeled, identifying at least three distinct shapes (e.g., linear, bent, tetrahedral).
task: Students use clay and toothpicks to build 3D models of 5 different molecules, starting from their Lewis structures, and label the geometry of each.

mastery_criterion: Observation log correctly matches chemical formulas to their VSEPR geometries.
task: Students use a safe, interactive digital simulation on tablets (that does not require student accounts or collect personal data) to build molecules and observe their 3D geometries, filling out an observation log.

mastery_criterion: Correct Lewis structure, accurate 3D clay model, and correct geometry name (tetrahedral).
task: Practical assessment where students are given a chemical formula (e.g., CH4), must draw the Lewis structure, build the clay model, and state the geometry name.

mastery_criterion: Students can explain why a symmetrical molecule with polar bonds has no net dipole.
task: Explain molecular polarity by combining bond polarity and 3D geometry. Use a physical tug-of-war analogy to show how symmetrical polar bonds cancel out.

mastery_criterion: Correct determination of polarity for at least 6 out of 8 molecules with logical justifications based on symmetry.
task: Students analyze a set of 8 molecules, determine their geometry, draw dipole arrows, and deduce if the overall molecule is polar or non-polar, justifying their choice.

mastery_criterion: Presentations clearly articulate the role of molecular symmetry in canceling or not canceling bond dipoles.
task: Students work in pairs to create a presentation explaining why water is polar but carbon tetrachloride is non-polar, using diagrams and written explanations.

mastery_criterion: Accurate polarity identification and scientifically sound written justifications mentioning symmetry and bond dipoles.
task: Written test requiring students to evaluate three given molecules, state their polarity, and write a paragraph justifying their answer using VSEPR and electronegativity concepts.

mastery_criterion: Students can list at least three signs of a chemical change and distinguish them from physical changes.
task: Demonstrate physical changes (tearing paper, melting ice) and safe chemical changes (vinegar and baking soda). Teach students to look for macroscopic evidence of chemical changes.

mastery_criterion: Accurate classification of all 5 stations with justifications based on observable evidence.
task: Students rotate through 5 safe stations (e.g., dissolving salt, mixing colored water, reacting antacid in water) to observe, record data, and deduce if a physical or chemical change occurred.

mastery_criterion: Correct classification and logical justification for at least 13 out of 15 scenarios.
task: Students read 15 short scenarios describing changes in matter and write a justification for whether each is physical or chemical.

mastery_criterion: Essay correctly identifies a chemical change and cites color change and new substance formation as evidence.
task: Students are given a scenario about an iron nail rusting and must write a short essay deciding if it is a physical or chemical change, justifying with evidence.

mastery_criterion: Students consistently move to the correct side and provide valid quick justifications.
task: Teacher reads quick scenarios aloud; students move to the left side of the room for 'physical' and the right side for 'chemical', then one student is randomly called to justify.

mastery_criterion: Score of 80% or higher on the quiz.
task: Students complete a 10-question multiple-choice quiz where they evaluate novel, brief scenarios and deduce if a physical or chemical change occurred based on evidence.

mastery_criterion: Students can label all parts of a provided chemical equation correctly.
task: Introduce the parts of a chemical equation. Show how to identify reactants, products, the yield arrow, and state symbols (s, l, g, aq).

mastery_criterion: Worksheet completed with 90% accuracy in identifying all components.
task: Students dissect 20 different chemical equations on a worksheet, circling reactants, underlining products, and listing the state symbols present.

mastery_criterion: Accurate translation of text to symbols and correct labeling of the equation parts.
task: Students translate written descriptions of chemical reactions into symbolic chemical equations, identifying the reactants, products, and states from the text.

mastery_criterion: Perfect identification of CaCO3 as reactant, CaO and CO2 as products, and gas as the state.
task: Given the equation CaCO3(s) + heat -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), students must write out the reactants, products, and the state of CO2 without reference materials.

mastery_criterion: Students can state the defining characteristics of the three taught reaction types.
task: Teach the patterns for classifying reactions into precipitation, neutralization, and displacement. Show generic formulas (e.g., Acid + Base -> Salt + Water).

mastery_criterion: Correct classification of at least 12 out of 15 equations.
task: Students analyze a set of 15 chemical equations and sort them into categories (precipitation, neutralization, displacement), providing a reason for each classification.

mastery_criterion: Accurate classification of the described reactions based on the text.
task: Students read descriptions of industrial and everyday chemical processes, write the basic equation, and classify the reaction type.

mastery_criterion: Correct classification of at least 8 out of 10 items.
task: Students are given 5 novel chemical equations and 5 text descriptions of reactions. They must classify all 10 into the correct categories.

mastery_criterion: Students can define both terms and explain the direction of heat flow for each.
task: Explain endothermic and exothermic reactions based on heat transfer. Demonstrate an exothermic reaction (safe hand warmers) and an endothermic one (baking soda and vinegar with a thermometer).

mastery_criterion: Accurate graphs and correct deduction of energy flow based on temperature data.
task: Students perform safe micro-scale reactions in cups, measure temperature changes over 5 minutes, graph the data, and deduce if the reaction is endothermic or exothermic.

mastery_criterion: Correct identification of reaction type and logical justification referencing the temperature change shown on the graph.
task: Students analyze provided temperature-time graphs of various unknown reactions, determine the energy type, and write a justification for each based on the graph's slope.

mastery_criterion: Correctly identifies the reaction as endothermic and justifies it by stating heat is absorbed from the surroundings.
task: Students read a scenario about mixing baking soda and vinegar where the container feels cold. They must determine if it is endothermic or exothermic and justify their answer in writing.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 3 out of 4 provided food examples into their primary biomolecule group.
task: Students will observe physical samples of common foods (e.g., oil, sugar, egg white) and read short texts describing their primary biomolecule components. They will create a three-column chart in their notebooks to list the characteristics of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, and classify the observed foods into these categories. The teacher will review the charts for accuracy.

mastery_criterion: Comic strip accurately depicts the enzyme remaining unchanged after the reaction.
task: Students will watch a teacher-led demonstration using a physical model (lock and key puzzle) to represent enzymes and substrates. They will then draw a comic strip in their notebooks illustrating an enzyme binding to a substrate, accelerating a reaction, and releasing products without being changed. The teacher will circulate to check the comic strips.

mastery_criterion: Venn diagram correctly places the nucleus and membrane-bound organelles in the eukaryotic section only.
task: Students will examine large printed diagrams of a bacterium and an animal cell. Working in pairs, they will use a checklist to identify which structures (nucleus, cell membrane, organelles) are present in each diagram. They will then construct a Venn diagram on poster paper comparing the two cell types. Posters will be displayed for a gallery walk.

mastery_criterion: Cards are glued in the correct hierarchical order from atom to organ.
task: Students will receive a set of cards with images and names of different biological levels (e.g., carbon atom, protein, red blood cell, muscle tissue, heart). They will work in small groups to physically arrange the cards in order of increasing complexity. They will then glue the sorted cards into their notebooks and write a one-sentence justification for the placement of the 'tissue' card.

mastery_criterion: Worksheet correctly identifies chloroplasts and cell walls as exclusive to the plant cell images.
task: Students will analyze micrographic images of plant leaves and human cheek cells provided by the teacher. They will complete a guided worksheet where they circle the cell wall and chloroplasts in the plant cell images and note their absence in the animal cell images. Finally, they will write a summary paragraph differentiating the two.

mastery_criterion: Diagrams correctly label ATP as an energy source and show a gradient as a difference in concentration.
task: Students will participate in a role-play activity where 'ATP tokens' are exchanged for 'cellular work' (e.g., moving a desk, lifting a book). The teacher will explain how breaking a bond in ATP releases energy. Students will then draw a diagram in their notebooks showing ATP converting to ADP to release energy, and a separate diagram showing a concentration gradient.

mastery_criterion: Graphic organizer correctly states that active transport requires energy and moves against the gradient.
task: Students will model passive and active transport using a cardboard box with a slit (membrane) and ping-pong balls (molecules). They will push balls through the slit from high to low concentration (passive) and then use 'energy' (a designated student pushing back) to move them from low to high concentration (active). They will record their observations and definitions in a graphic organizer.

mastery_criterion: Conclusion accurately predicts cell shrinking in hypertonic and swelling in hypotonic solutions, citing the potato evidence.
task: Students will observe a teacher demonstration of potato slices placed in pure water (hypotonic) and very salty water (hypertonic) prepared the day before. They will measure the flexibility and size of the slices, record the data, and write a conclusion predicting what would happen to a human cell in similar conditions based on the evidence.

mastery_criterion: Flowchart correctly shows glucose and oxygen entering the mitochondria, and ATP, water, and CO2 exiting.
task: Students will create a flowchart using cut-out shapes representing glucose, oxygen, mitochondria, ATP, water, and carbon dioxide. They will arrange the shapes to show the inputs and outputs of aerobic respiration. Once approved by the teacher, they will glue the flowchart into their notebooks and write a descriptive caption.

mastery_criterion: Paragraph explicitly states that light provides energy to split water for glucose production.
task: Students will analyze a diagram of a chloroplast showing light hitting it, water entering, and oxygen and glucose being produced. They will work in pairs to answer a set of guided questions about the diagram, focusing on the role of light as an energy source to split water. They will then write a short explanatory paragraph.

mastery_criterion: Map and explanation correctly sequence the pathway: Rough ER -> Golgi -> Cell Membrane.
task: Students will draw a large map of a cell on poster paper, labeling the nucleus, rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and cell membrane. They will use a small token (representing a protein) and physically move it along the pathway, drawing arrows to trace its route. They will present their map to another group, explaining the journey.

mastery_criterion: Table correctly links biomolecules to structures and assigns the correct organizational level.
task: Students will complete a matching activity where they link specific biomolecules (e.g., a specific protein) to the cellular structures they form, and then place those structures into the correct level of organization. They will record their matches in a structured table.

mastery_criterion: Lab report correctly identifies the tap water as hypotonic (causing swelling) and salt water as hypertonic.
task: Students will design a simple experiment using gummy bears placed in tap water and salt water. They will write a hypothesis predicting the outcome based on osmosis, leave the setup overnight (time not counted in minutes), and analyze the results the next day, writing a formal lab report.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the biomolecule group for at least 80% of the flashcards.
task: Students will play a flashcard game in pairs. One student reads the characteristics of a biomolecule, and the other must name the group (carbohydrate, lipid, or protein). They will track their correct answers and review any missed cards.

mastery_criterion: Quiz correctly identifies the primary biomolecule for at least two of the three foods.
task: Students will complete a short written quiz where they must list three foods they ate recently and identify the primary biomolecule in each, justifying their choice based on the characteristics learned.

mastery_criterion: Correctly predicts water movement and tonicity for at least two of the three scenarios.
task: Students will be given three scenarios on a worksheet (e.g., a plant wilting, a slug with salt on it, a red blood cell in pure water). They must predict the direction of water movement and state whether the environment is hypertonic or hypotonic.

mastery_criterion: Student's written response correctly identifies a hypertonic solution and justifies it with water leaving the cell.
task: Students will participate in a 'think-pair-share' activity. The teacher will project an image of a shriveled cell. Students will individually write down their prediction of what type of solution caused this, pair up to discuss their reasoning, and then share with the class.

mastery_criterion: Scores at least 70% overall, with correct responses on the core essay connecting photosynthesis products to respiration inputs.
task: Students will complete a comprehensive written exam covering biomolecules, cell types, and energy processes. The exam includes multiple-choice questions, diagram labeling, and short essay responses requiring them to connect photosynthesis and respiration.

mastery_criterion: Model accurately depicts the cyclical relationship between the two processes.
task: Students will create a conceptual model showing how the outputs of photosynthesis (glucose, oxygen) become the inputs for cellular respiration, and vice versa. They will write a paragraph explaining how this cycle sustains life on Earth, bridging cellular processes to ecosystem dynamics.

mastery_criterion: Posters accurately identify the substrate and products, and explicitly state that the enzyme is not consumed in the reaction.
task: Students will work in small groups to analyze three different scenarios where enzymes are used in everyday life (e.g., digestion, laundry detergents, fruit browning). They will create a poster for one scenario, illustrating the specific substrate, the enzyme's role, and the resulting products, emphasizing that the enzyme is reusable.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize at least 80% of the mystery cell cards and provide accurate structural justifications.
task: Students will be given a set of 'mystery cell' profile cards containing descriptions of cellular structures. They must sort the cards into 'Prokaryotic', 'Eukaryotic', or 'Both' categories, and then write a short justification for each placement in their notebooks.

mastery_criterion: Models accurately include chloroplasts and cell walls for plant cells, or omit them for animal cells, with correct labels.
task: Students will use modeling clay to build 3D models of either a plant or an animal cell. They must include and label the specific organelles that differentiate their chosen cell type from the other, and then pair up with a student who built the opposite type to compare models.

mastery_criterion: Worksheets correctly map the analogies to ATP and gradients, demonstrating an understanding of stored vs. released energy.
task: Students will complete a worksheet featuring analogies for cellular energy (e.g., a charged battery vs. a dead battery, water behind a dam vs. flowing water). They must map these analogies to ATP/ADP cycles and chemical gradients, explaining how each represents biologically useful energy.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort the scenarios and can verbally explain that active transport requires ATP while passive does not.
task: Students will participate in a sorting relay race. They will be given cards describing various cellular transport scenarios (e.g., oxygen entering a cell, a pump moving sodium out). They must run to the board and place their card under the correct heading: 'Active Transport' or 'Passive Transport'.

mastery_criterion: Stories accurately include the mitochondria, oxygen, and the production of ATP as the main goal of the process.
task: Students will write a creative short story from the perspective of a glucose molecule entering a cell. The story must describe the molecule's journey to the mitochondria, its interaction with oxygen, and its ultimate transformation into ATP, water, and carbon dioxide.

mastery_criterion: Comic strips accurately depict light as the energy source for splitting water and producing sugars.
task: Students will create a comic strip illustrating the process of photosynthesis. The comic must clearly show light energy being used to split water molecules, and the subsequent use of those components to build glucose from carbon dioxide.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully navigate the board game pathway (ER -> Golgi -> Membrane) and answer pathway-related questions correctly.
task: Students will play a board game designed by the teacher where they act as 'cellular delivery drivers'. They must roll dice to move their protein cargo from the rough ER, through the Golgi apparatus, and out of the cell membrane, answering review questions to advance.

mastery_criterion: Quizzes correctly define enzymes as reusable biological catalysts that act on substrates.
task: Students will complete a quick-fire quiz where they must define an enzyme, identify its target (substrate), and state whether it is consumed in a reaction. They will then swap papers and grade each other's work based on a teacher-provided rubric.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the level of organization for at least 80% of the called-out structures.
task: Students will participate in a 'whiteboard shootout'. The teacher will call out a biological structure (e.g., 'heart', 'carbon', 'red blood cell'), and students must quickly write the correct level of organization on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up.

mastery_criterion: Paragraphs correctly use the terms 'ATP', 'active', 'passive', and 'gradient' in the proper context.
task: Students will complete a 'fill-in-the-blanks' paragraph summarizing the differences between active and passive transport, focusing on the use of ATP and the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient.

mastery_criterion: Diagrams accurately show the correct inputs and outputs of aerobic respiration in the mitochondria.
task: Students will draw a simple diagram from memory showing a mitochondrion, with arrows indicating what goes in (glucose, oxygen) and what comes out (ATP, water, carbon dioxide).

mastery_criterion: Students score at least 70% on the assessment, demonstrating solid foundational knowledge before moving to complex cellular processes.
task: Students will complete a mid-unit written assessment covering biomolecules, enzymes, cell types, and levels of organization. The test will include multiple-choice questions, matching sections, and short-answer questions requiring them to apply their knowledge to new examples.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly draw and label the three components of a nucleotide with appropriate color-coding.
task: Introduce the three components of a DNA nucleotide using a large board diagram. Students draw their own nucleotide in their notebooks, color-coding the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base, and write a one-sentence definition for each part.

mastery_criterion: The 3D model accurately reflects the structural connection between the phosphate, sugar, and base.
task: Students use modeling clay to build a 3D model of a single nucleotide. They must select three different colors to represent the phosphate, sugar, and base, assemble them in the correct structural arrangement, and present their model to a partner.

mastery_criterion: All three components are correctly identified on at least two of the three diagrams regardless of orientation.
task: Students receive a worksheet with three different blank diagrams of nucleotides in various orientations. They must correctly label the phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, and nitrogenous base on all three diagrams.

mastery_criterion: The Venn diagram correctly places 'nucleus' under eukaryotic, 'nucleoid region' under prokaryotic, and 'contains DNA' in the overlapping section.
task: Present side-by-side diagrams of a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell. Explain the difference between a nucleus and a nucleoid region. Students create a Venn diagram comparing where DNA is stored in both cell types.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 8 out of 10 cards into the proper DNA location categories.
task: Students are given 10 cards with descriptions of different cells (e.g., 'A human skin cell', 'A bacterium found in soil'). They must sort the cards into 'Eukaryotic (Nucleus)' and 'Prokaryotic (Nucleoid)' categories based on prior knowledge of organisms and the new DNA location rules.

mastery_criterion: The response explicitly states that plant cell DNA is in the nucleus and bacterial DNA is in the nucleoid region.
task: Students write a short paragraph answering the prompt: 'If you were a scientist looking for DNA in a plant cell versus a bacterial cell, where exactly would you look in each, and why?'

mastery_criterion: Students hypothesize that without detergent, the membranes will not break, and DNA will remain trapped inside the cell.
task: Demonstrate a virtual or video-based plant DNA extraction. Pause the video before the detergent step. Explain the lipid nature of cell membranes and how soap interacts with lipids. Students write a hypothesis about what would happen if this step were skipped.

mastery_criterion: Students successfully document that the soap was required to break down the lipid membrane to access the DNA.
task: Students perform a safe, hands-on DNA extraction using strawberries (or bananas), salt, dish soap, and cold rubbing alcohol. They mash the fruit, mix it with the soap/salt solution to break down lipid membranes, filter it, and add cold alcohol to precipitate the DNA, documenting how the soap was necessary.

mastery_criterion: The review identifies the missing detergent, explains its role in breaking lipid membranes, and predicts that no DNA will be extracted.
task: Students are given a flawed protocol for DNA extraction that omits the detergent step. They must write a critical review of the protocol, identifying the missing step, explaining its purpose based on cell structure, and predicting the outcome of the flawed protocol.

mastery_criterion: The comic strip shows the four stages in the correct chronological order with accurate visual representations of the chromosomes.
task: The teacher performs a live demonstration of preparing an onion root tip squash, explaining the process of staining and pressing to see cells. Then, introduce the four main stages of mitosis using large printed micrographs of onion root tip cells on the board. Explain the visual hallmarks of each stage (condensing, aligning, separating, dividing). Students create a four-panel comic strip illustrating these stages in order.

mastery_criterion: Pairs successfully create at least two complete, correctly ordered timelines from prophase to telophase.
task: Students are given a mixed set of 12 micrographs showing various cells in different stages of mitosis. Working in pairs, they must identify the stage of each cell and arrange them into three complete, sequential timelines of mitosis.

mastery_criterion: All four images are pasted in the exact correct sequence, and justifications match the visual evidence.
task: Students receive an assessment sheet with four out-of-order micrographs of mitosis. They must cut them out, paste them in the correct sequence on a new sheet, and write a one-sentence justification for the placement of each image.

mastery_criterion: Students can arrange the four stages in the correct order without hesitation.
task: Flashcard speed-sort: Students receive a shuffled deck of mitosis stage images and must arrange them in the correct order as quickly as possible, repeating the process three times to improve their speed.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly calculate that the chromosome number would double each generation (92, 184, 368) if mitosis produced gametes.
task: Use a bead model to demonstrate chromosome numbers. Show a cell with 46 beads dividing by mitosis (resulting in 46) versus meiosis (resulting in 23). Walk through a hypothetical scenario on the board showing what happens if two 46-chromosome gametes fuse. Students calculate the resulting chromosome numbers for three generations under this hypothetical scenario.

mastery_criterion: The poster clearly contrasts the outcome of fertilization with diploid vs. haploid gametes and justifies meiosis as the mechanism for maintaining species chromosome numbers.
task: Students work in groups to create a poster explaining 'The Meiosis Solution'. They must visually depict the problem of chromosome doubling and how meiosis solves it by halving the number before fertilization. They must include a written justification.

mastery_criterion: The response predicts the doubling of chromosomes (to 92) and justifies this by explaining that mitosis does not halve the chromosome number like meiosis does.
task: Students answer a written prompt: 'Predict what would happen to the chromosome number of a human offspring if gametes were produced by mitosis instead of meiosis. Justify your answer using the concepts of fertilization and chromosome sets.'

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the reproduction type for all three scenarios and cite the presence or absence of two parents/genetic exchange.
task: Define sexual and asexual reproduction focusing on genetic exchange. Read three distinct scenarios aloud (yeast budding, human fertilization, bacterial fission). For each, students hold up a 'Sexual' or 'Asexual' card and write down the key phrase from the scenario that justifies their choice.

mastery_criterion: At least 13 out of 15 case studies are correctly classified with appropriate evidence underlined.
task: Students are given a set of 15 short case studies of different organisms reproducing. They must classify each case into a T-chart (Sexual vs. Asexual) and underline the evidence in the text that led to their decision.

mastery_criterion: All three scenarios are correctly classified with a valid explanation referencing genetic exchange or parent number.
task: Students read three new, unseen scenarios of organism reproduction. They must write a short paragraph for each, classifying it as sexual or asexual and explaining why based on genetic exchange.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the seed as sexual and the tuber/graft as asexual in their drawings.
task: Explain the difference between growing plants from seeds (sexual) and vegetative parts (asexual). Show physical examples or high-quality images of a bean seed, a potato tuber, and a grafted branch. Students draw each method and label it as sexual or asexual.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize maize propagation as sexual and potato tubers as asexual based on the text.
task: Using the local-crops context, students analyze agricultural fact sheets about how maize (grown from seed) and potatoes (grown from tubers) are propagated in El Salvador. They must categorize the methods described in the fact sheets into sexual and asexual reproduction.

mastery_criterion: All five actions are correctly sorted into the sexual (seeds/pits) and asexual (rhizomes, cuttings, bulbs) categories.
task: Students are given a list of five plant propagation actions (e.g., planting a sunflower seed, burying a piece of ginger rhizome, planting a mango pit, taking a rose cutting, planting a bulb). They must sort them into a table under 'Sexual' or 'Asexual'.

mastery_criterion: The written rule accurately states that if gametes meet outside the body (usually in water), it is external; if inside, it is internal.
task: Define internal and external fertilization based on where gametes meet. Use a diagram of a fish spawning in water versus a mammal. Students write a rule in their notebooks for determining the type of fertilization based on the environment described.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the fertilization type for all three animals and cite the environmental meeting place of gametes as evidence.
task: Using the protected-areas context, students read fact sheets about three animals found in San Salvador volcano protected areas (e.g., a specific tree frog, a snake, a bird). They must determine if each uses internal or external fertilization based on clues about where the eggs and sperm meet, and write a justification.

mastery_criterion: The student identifies external fertilization and explains that it is because the sperm and egg meet in the river water, outside the mother's body.
task: Students read a short paragraph about a newly discovered aquatic species that releases thousands of eggs into a river, followed by a male releasing sperm over them. They must state whether this is internal or external fertilization and explain why.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly label the shell as protection and the yolk as the nutrient/energy source.
task: Crack open an unfertilized chicken egg into a petri dish (teacher demonstration). Identify the shell, yolk, and albumen. Explain the function of each for a developing embryo. Students draw the egg and write the survival function next to the shell and yolk.

mastery_criterion: The design includes a protective outer layer (shell equivalent) and an internal energy source (yolk equivalent), with a logical explanation of their functions.
task: Students are given a design challenge: 'Design a synthetic egg for a robotic embryo.' They must draw their design, explicitly including a structure that acts like a shell and a structure that acts like a yolk, and write a paragraph explaining how their synthetic parts perform the same survival functions as the biological ones.

mastery_criterion: The student states that the yolk provides energy to grow, and the shell provides protection.
task: Students answer two questions: 1) What is the function of the yolk for a bird embryo? 2) What is the function of the shell? They must state their answers based on the functions of these structures.

mastery_criterion: Sketches clearly show the blastula as a simple hollow circle of cells and the gastrula with an inward fold.
task: Explain the transition from a single cell to a blastula (hollow ball) and then a gastrula (folded/layered ball). Demonstrate this using a deflated rubber ball: show it round (blastula), then push one side in (gastrula). Students sketch the two stages and label the key difference (hollow vs. folded).

mastery_criterion: The physical clay models, when cut, accurately display a hollow center for the blastula and an inward fold for the gastrula.
task: Students use modeling clay to create a physical model of a blastula and a gastrula. They must slice their models in half (using a plastic safe knife or string) to reveal the cross-section, proving that the blastula is hollow and the gastrula has an invagination.

mastery_criterion: The drawings correctly depict the hollow blastula and the invaginated gastrula, and the sentence describes the folding/layering process.
task: Students are given two blank circles on a page. They must draw the cellular cross-section of a blastula in the first circle and a gastrula in the second circle, then write one sentence stating the physical difference between the two.

mastery_criterion: Students consistently draw the correct structure (hollow vs. folded) within the time limit.
task: Whiteboard quick-draw: The teacher calls out either 'Blastula' or 'Gastrula'. Students have 30 seconds to draw the correct cross-section on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up. Repeat for several rounds to build speed and accuracy.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and sort the models based on the presence of a hollow center or an invagination.
task: Students are given a mixed set of clay models (some blastulas, some gastrulas, some incorrect shapes) prepared by the teacher. They must quickly sort them into 'Blastula', 'Gastrula', and 'Incorrect' piles based on their structural features.

mastery_criterion: The model accurately represents the three components and their connections.
task: Students use recycled materials (bottle caps, straws, cardboard) to construct a large-scale model of a nucleotide, labeling the phosphate, sugar, and base.

mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize 90% of the descriptions.
task: Students play a rapid-fire sorting game on the board, categorizing cell descriptions into 'Nucleus' or 'Nucleoid'.

mastery_criterion: The report correctly calculates the exponential growth of chromosomes and justifies why meiosis is necessary.
task: Students analyze a hypothetical alien species that reproduces using mitosis for gametes. They must calculate the chromosome number over 5 generations and write a scientific report on why this species would face genetic instability.

mastery_criterion: The garden plan correctly identifies the propagation method for each plant and categorizes it accurately.
task: Students design a community garden plan using the local-crops context, selecting specific propagation methods (seeds for maize, tubers for potatoes) and justifying their choices as sexual or asexual.
